body:
Gujarat before Mughal conquest

Before its incorporation into the Mughal Empire, Gujarat was governed by the Gujarat Sultanate, an important regional kingdom with Ahmedabad as its capital. The region possessed productive agricultural lands, established textile industries and ports connected to overseas trade.

Gujarat was valuable because its commercial centres connected the interior of India with the Arabian Sea. Merchants could bring goods from inland production centres to its ports and exchange them with traders from West Asia, Africa and other regions. Control over Gujarat therefore offered a ruler both land revenue and income associated with commerce.

Akbar's conquest of Gujarat

Emperor Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, extended Mughal authority into Gujarat through campaigns in 1572–1573. The Gujarat Sultanate lost its independent political position, and Gujarat was incorporated into the Mughal Empire.

An important event was Akbar's capture of Surat fort in February 1573. Surat was already a significant trading centre. Its incorporation brought an important commercial gateway under Mughal authority.

After the conquest, Gujarat was organised as a Mughal province, or suba, with Ahmedabad serving as its principal administrative centre.

Why Gujarat was important to the Mughal Empire

The value of Gujarat rested on the relationship between its countryside, manufacturing towns and ports:

  • Agriculture: Cultivators produced food crops and commercial crops such as cotton and indigo.
  • Manufacturing: Artisans converted raw materials into textiles and other marketable goods.
  • Inland commerce: Merchants connected villages and manufacturing towns with larger markets.
  • Maritime commerce: Ports such as Surat and Khambat connected Gujarat to overseas buyers.
  • Revenue: Agricultural taxation and commercial activity provided resources for imperial administration.

The conquest did not mean that every local chief immediately lost authority. Mughal officials governed some territories directly, while local rulers and landed intermediaries retained important responsibilities elsewhere. This distinction is essential for understanding provincial administration.

Ahmedabad and Surat had different principal roles. Ahmedabad was the administrative centre of Mughal Gujarat and an important manufacturing city. Surat was a major maritime trading port. Both were commercially important, but they were not interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • Akbar's reign: 1556–1605.
  • Major Mughal campaigns in Gujarat: 1572–1573.
  • Akbar captured Surat fort in February 1573.
  • Gujarat became a Mughal suba, with Ahmedabad as its principal administrative centre.
  • The region's importance included agriculture, textiles, ports and revenue.
  • Trap: Surat was a major port, not the provincial capital.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, The Mughal Empire, pp. 47–48 and 53–54; Gujarat Government, NRI Division, History of Surat, section on Akbar's conquest, consulted 19 November 2026; IGNOU, MHI-10, Unit 30, Cities in the 18th Century-1, section 30.4, Ahmadabad, p. 59, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: The Establishment of Mughal Rule in Gujarat

body:
The suba as a unit of government

The Mughal Empire was divided into large provinces called subas. Each suba was governed in the emperor's name, but the administration depended on several officers with different responsibilities.

Gujarat formed one such province. Ahmedabad was its principal administrative centre. Within the province, smaller territorial divisions helped officials supervise revenue collection, local order and imperial instructions.

Administrative divisions below the province

The main territorial divisions were:

  • Suba: A province of the Mughal Empire, such as Gujarat.
  • Sarkar: A territorial division below the suba, commonly comparable to a district-level unit.
  • Pargana or mahal: A smaller administrative or revenue unit containing villages and cultivated lands.
  • Village: The local settlement and an important level for agricultural production and revenue information.

Following Mughal conquest, Gujarat was reorganised into 16 sarkars. Of these, 9 came under direct Mughal administrative and fiscal control, while the remaining 7 remained under local chiefs. This arrangement demonstrates that incorporation into the empire did not necessarily mean identical administration in every locality.

Principal officers and their functions

OfficeMain responsibility
SubadarGovernor responsible for provincial political and military administration.
DiwanFinancial officer responsible for revenue administration and accounts.
BakhshiOfficer concerned with military payments and related military administration.
FaujdarMilitary commander concerned with security and enforcement in an assigned area.
KotwalOfficer responsible for policing and maintaining order in a town.
SadrOfficer concerned with religious and charitable patronage.

The difference between the subadar and diwan

The subadar exercised provincial political and military authority. The diwan supervised the financial side of provincial government, particularly revenue and accounts. Their functions were related but distinct.

Revenue was essential for maintaining the army and government. Keeping political-military authority and financial supervision in separate offices helped the emperor monitor powerful provincial officers.

Local administration and imperial authority

Imperial orders did not reach cultivators and merchants through the governor alone. Sarkar-level officers, revenue officials, local chiefs, village headmen and zamindars helped connect the provincial government with the population.

Surat's importance as a major port also required attention to commercial revenue and security. Its local government operated within the wider Mughal provincial system, while the imperial government retained a strong interest in its port and fort.

A subadar governed the province; a diwan supervised its finances; a faujdar performed military and security duties in an assigned area; and a kotwal maintained order in a town.

Prelims focus

  • Suba means province; sarkar is a division below the province.
  • Pargana and mahal were smaller administrative or revenue units.
  • Ahmedabad was the principal administrative centre of Mughal Gujarat.
  • Gujarat was reorganised into 16 sarkars: 9 directly administered by the Mughals and 7 under local chiefs.
  • Subadar: political and military administration; diwan: finance and revenue.
  • Trap: The subadar and diwan were not names for the same office.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, The Mughal Empire, pp. 53–54; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, pp. 213–218; IGNOU, MHI-10, Unit 30, Cities in the 18th Century-1, section 30.4, Ahmadabad, p. 59, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Provincial Administration of Mughal Gujarat

body:
Why agricultural revenue mattered

Agriculture provided a major part of the Mughal Empire's income. Cultivators produced crops, while government officials and local intermediaries assessed and collected revenue. The income supported imperial expenditure, including the administration and military establishment.

In Gujarat, cultivated land also supplied cotton and indigo for commercial production. Agriculture therefore supported both the government's revenue system and the region's textile trade.

The mansabdari system

A mansab was a rank or position held by an imperial officer. A person holding such a rank was called a mansabdar.

The system connected an officer's position, remuneration and military obligations:

  • Zat: The numerical rank indicating a mansabdar's personal standing and salary.
  • Sawar: The cavalry-related rank indicating the number of horsemen the mansabdar was required to maintain.
  • Jagir: A revenue assignment from which a mansabdar could receive income in place of a cash salary.

A jagir normally gave its holder the right to receive revenue from assigned territory. It did not automatically make the mansabdar the private owner of all the land or an independent ruler. Many mansabdars served in one part of the empire while receiving revenue from jagirs situated elsewhere.

Zamindars and rural intermediaries

Zamindars were local landed intermediaries who could possess land, exercise influence in rural society and collect revenue on behalf of the state. Some were village headmen; others were powerful chiefs with substantial territories and armed followers.

A zamindar and a jagirdar were therefore not necessarily the same. A zamindar's influence arose from local landed and customary rights, while a jagirdar received a state-assigned claim to revenue as part of the imperial service system.

Assessment and collection of land revenue

Under Akbar, revenue minister Raja Todar Mal organised a system of assessment using information on cultivated area, crop yields and prices. The survey used data gathered over the period 1570–1580. Crop-wise revenue rates could then be fixed in cash.

This arrangement was called zabt. It required reliable land measurement, crop information and accounts. Such conditions did not exist uniformly across the empire. In particular, the system could not be applied throughout provinces such as Gujarat and Bengal in the same manner as in areas where detailed measurement was practicable.

The difficulty of applying zabt uniformly in Gujarat did not mean that Gujarat was exempt from Mughal land revenue. It meant that assessment and collection arrangements had to take account of local conditions and available information.

Jama and hasil

Two terms distinguish what the government expected from what it actually obtained:

  • Jama: The amount of land revenue assessed or demanded.
  • Hasil: The amount of revenue actually collected.

These amounts could differ. Difficult cultivation conditions, local opposition or weaknesses in collection could prevent officials from realising the full assessed demand.

Effects on the countryside

Revenue demands linked cultivators, zamindars, collectors and imperial officers. If officials or jagirdars attempted to collect excessively, cultivators could face hardship. Powerful local intermediaries could also resist government demands, making the countryside an important area of negotiation and conflict.

Prelims focus

  • Mansabdar means holder of a Mughal rank.
  • Zat indicated personal rank and salary; sawar indicated cavalry obligations.
  • Jagir meant a revenue assignment, not automatic private ownership of the assigned territory.
  • Todar Mal's revenue assessment used data from 1570–1580.
  • Zabt could not be applied uniformly in provinces such as Gujarat and Bengal.
  • Jama means assessed revenue; hasil means revenue actually collected.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, The Mughal Empire, pp. 51–53; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, sections 5–6, pp. 211–215.]

title: Mansabdars, Jagirs and Land Revenue in Gujarat

body:
How towns supported regional trade

Gujarat's economy depended on a network of agricultural villages, manufacturing towns, inland markets and ports. These places performed related but different functions. Some were centres of administration and craft production; others connected inland merchants with overseas shipping.

A product made in one town could be sold through merchants in another and exported from a port. A major commercial centre was therefore not necessarily the place where every exported item was manufactured.

Important commercial centres and their functions

CentreLocation or characterPrincipal importance
AhmedabadInland cityMughal provincial administration, textile manufacture, indigo and textile procurement.
SuratTapi river and western maritime tradeMajor overseas trading port, warehouses, merchant finance and pilgrim departures.
Khambat (Cambay)Gulf of KhambhatEstablished centre of western Indian maritime commerce.
Bharuch (Broach)Narmada river regionTrading and textile-producing centre connected with wider commercial routes.
Baroda (Vadodara)Inland GujaratCommercial and textile-producing centre; later an important Gaekwad centre.

Ahmedabad as a manufacturing and administrative city

Ahmedabad brought together officials, merchants and artisans. Textile producers worked in and around the city, while merchant networks arranged the purchase of cloth and indigo.

European trading companies also established commercial establishments in Ahmedabad during the 17th century. They procured goods from the city and its surrounding manufacturing region rather than conducting all their business directly at the seacoast.

Surat and Khambat as maritime gateways

Surat became especially prominent as the Mughal period's great western trading emporium. An emporium is a commercial centre where goods from several producing regions are brought together for exchange or sale.

Khambat, also called Cambay in older accounts, was another established centre of western trade. Its position on the Gulf of Khambhat connected Gujarat's commercial networks with the Arabian Sea.

Although both cities participated in maritime commerce, Surat became particularly important for the large-scale overseas trade and pilgrim shipping of the Mughal period.

Links between production centres and ports

The land between Ahmedabad and Surat supported crops such as cotton and indigo. Cotton was processed into yarn and cloth, while indigo was used as a dye. Artisans in commercial towns produced goods that merchants could send to ports for export.

Trade therefore connected agricultural production, craft employment, transport and overseas demand. Merchants and bankers helped organise this movement of goods and payments.

Ahmedabad: administration and manufacture. Surat: major overseas port. Khambat: established Gulf of Khambhat trading centre. These are related but distinct roles.

Prelims focus

  • Ahmedabad was an important Mughal administrative and textile-producing city.
  • Surat was a major western maritime trading port.
  • Cambay is the historical name used for Khambat.
  • Bharuch is associated with the Narmada region.
  • Cotton, indigo, textiles and merchant networks supported Gujarat's regional trade.
  • Trap: The main port of export need not have been the place where an exported textile was woven.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, pp. 79–85; IGNOU, MHI-10, Unit 30, Cities in the 18th Century-1, section 30.4, Ahmadabad, pp. 59–60, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: How Gujarat's agricultural and manufacturing centres connected with inland markets and maritime ports.

title: The Commercial Centres of Mughal Gujarat
